title: StochLOB: Heavy-Tailed Score Matching for Robust Limit Order Book Trend Prediction

paper.title: StochLOB: Heavy-Tailed Score Matching for Robust Limit Order Book Trend Prediction
paper.abstract:
Abstract Score-based diffusion methods usually perturb data with Brownian Gaussian
noise, corresponding to a light-tailed forward stochastic differential
equation (SDE). For market time series this SDE can be a poor abstraction:
limit order book (LOB) order flow is heavy-tailed, bursty, and occasionally
jump-like. We study StochLOB , a training-only score-matching
framework that changes the forward diffusion corruption law while leaving the
deployed predictor deterministic. Instead of Brownian-only Gaussian
corruption, the noising process uses two non-Gaussian SDE-inspired
alternatives: jump- Lévy noise through a compound-Poisson variance
mixture, and clipped α \alpha -stable noise through a positive-stable
Gaussian scale mixture. These corruptions inject finite jumps and
heavy-tailed residuals into training without requiring reverse-time diffusion
sampling at inference. The resulting score target has a useful
interpretation: its radial factor h t ​ ( r ) h_{t}(r) is the posterior expected
corruption precision, so large residuals are weighted according to the latent
corruption scale that most plausibly generated them. On chronologically
held-out Coinbase LOB data, the proposed variants remain competitive on
uncorrupted BTC and altcoin test horizons and improve several realized
tail-window stress diagnostics. An exploratory Feishu A-share transfer study
further tests whether the probability outputs remain usable under transaction
costs and trading-rule constraints. Code and configuration files are
available at https://github.com/ArshiAbolghasemi/Penny .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Score-based diffusion methods are commonly built around a Brownian forward stochastic differential equation (SDE), whose finite-time corruption is Gaussian and light-tailed. This modeling choice is convenient, but it also defines the residual geometry seen by a denoising score objective: large coordinate movements become exponentially unlikely, and the learned restoring force is tied to a Brownian quadratic penalty. For data generated by stochastic systems with bursts, jumps, or persistent heavy tails, the Brownian-only SDE can therefore be a poor training corruption law. Limit order book (LOB) prediction makes this mismatch concrete. Order-flow imbalance (OFI), depth changes, and short-horizon returns can remain quiet for many bins and then move abruptly after an order sweep, a liquidity withdrawal, or a short burst of directional trading. These large residuals are not rare under the market process, but they are rare under Gaussian diffusion corruption. This is difficult to reconcile with the heavy tails and jump-like behavior observed in financial time series and LOB order flow ( Mandelbrot, 1963 ; Cont, 2001 ; Cont et al., 2014 ) . The question we study is whether the forward diffusion SDE used for score-based regularization should be modified so its noise law better matches the stochastic input process. We introduce StochLOB , a training-only framework for robust mid-price trend prediction. The deployed model remains a standard classifier: the corruption sampler and score head are used only while learning the shared representation, and test-time inference is a single deterministic forward pass. This isolates the effect of changing the stochastic diffusion corruption from the cost of reverse-time diffusion sampling at deployment. We consider two non-Gaussian SDE-inspired corruption families. The jump- Lévy variant adds a compound-Poisson jump component to a Brownian background, implemented as a Gaussian scale mixture that exposes the representation to mostly ordinary perturbations with occasional finite jumps. The α \alpha -stable variant replaces the fixed Brownian variance with a clipped positive-stable scale mixture, producing broad heavy-tailed perturbations while retaining numerical stability. Both variants use the same classifier architecture and differ only in the stochastic training law and auxiliary loss. The score target is also interpretable: the radial score factor h t ​ ( r ) h_{t}(r) is a posterior precision under the latent corruption scale. Thus the denoising objective does not apply the same restoring force to every residual. Ordinary residuals receive high posterior precision, while extreme residuals can be explained by larger latent corruption scales. Our empirical analysis follows the same logic. First, distribution-fit and tail diagnostics on Coinbase OFI show that the Gaussian assumption is a poor description of the observed inputs. Second, on Coinbase BTC and four additional crypto symbols, the proposed variants remain competitive on standard held-out mid-price trend prediction and win selected horizons, showing that the stochastic auxiliary objective does not require a large standard-test accuracy tradeoff. Third, realized stress-window diagnostics evaluate the regimes that motivate the method: high-stress, high-variance, and jump-residual windows in which Gaussian corruption is least plausible. Figure 1 gives the headline stress diagnostic at k = 100 k=100 . We also include an exploratory Feishu A-share transfer study in which model probabilities are converted into constrained portfolio signals, checking whether the forecasts remain useful after transaction costs, lot-size rules, and T+1 selling constraints. This transfer check is not meant to define a complete trading system; it tests whether the learned probabilities survive a realistic downstream decision rule. Contributions. We make three contributions. First, we formulate robust supervised representation learning as a mismatch between Brownian diffusion-SDE corruption and heavy-tailed, jump-like stochastic inputs, using LOB trend prediction as the concrete test bed. Second, we modify the training-time diffusion corruption with jump- Lévy and clipped α \alpha -stable noise while keeping the LOB predictor deterministic and free of inference-time sampling. Third, we provide a posterior-precision interpretation of the resulting score function h t h_{t} , with proofs and future-work mathematics in Appendix G . Appendices A – F provide the data details, score-table construction, implementation and training algorithms, additional crypto results, and the Feishu portfolio analysis. sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: LOB trend prediction. LOB forecasting has moved from linear models toward architectures that exploit both level structure and temporal order. DeepLOB combines convolutional, Inception, and recurrent blocks for mid-price movement prediction ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) . TABL and BiN-TABL add bilinear mappings, temporal attention, and input normalization for financial time series ( Tran et al., 2019 ; Tran et al., 2021 ) . Later work studies stronger attention and benchmarking designs, including TLOB, LiT, LOBench, Axial-LOB, and order-flow attention networks ( Berti and Kasneci, 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2025 ; Kisiel and Gorse, 2022 ; Bandealinaeini et al., 2025 ) . Our experiments keep the standard three-class mid-price trend protocol and compare against linear, recurrent, convolutional-attention, transformer, and single-asset order-flow attention baselines trained on the same chronological windows. Heavy tails and jumps. Heavy tails are a classical stylized fact of financial returns ( Mandelbrot, 1963 ; Cont, 2001 ) ; LOB-specific studies show non-Gaussian behavior in liquidity, impact, and order flow ( Bouchaud et al., 2002 ; Mike and Farmer, 2008 ; Gould et al., 2013 ; Cont et al., 2014 ) . Jump-diffusion models provide a finite-activity language for abrupt price moves ( Merton, 1976 ) , while stable processes model persistent heavy-tailed fluctuations ( Samorodnitsky and Taqqu, 1994 ) . We use these objects as training-time corruption laws, not as complete market simulators. Diffusion as representation learning. Score-based and denoising diffusion models are typically introduced as generative models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) , but the denoising task can also shape supervised representations. Joint diffusion training uses shared networks for denoising and prediction ( Deja et al., 2023 ) , and related work studies diffusion features as representation learners ( Yang and Wang, 2023 ) . Non-Gaussian diffusion replaces Brownian noise with jump or heavy-tailed processes ( Yoon et al., 2023 ; Shariatian et al., 2025 ; Pandey et al., 2025 ) . LOB diffusion work models event streams, counterfactual books, or volume snapshots ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Wang and Ventre, 2026 ; Wang and Ventre, 2025 ) ; StochLOB instead uses non-Gaussian corruption as a training-time auxiliary regularizer for deterministic LOB classification.

sections.heading: 3 Background
sections.text: Limit order book (LOB) data record the outstanding limit orders waiting at an exchange. At any time, the book has a bid side, where traders are willing to buy, and an ask side, where traders are willing to sell. Each side is ordered by price into levels: the first bid and ask levels are the immediately executable quotes, while deeper levels describe nearby liquidity that would be reached after the top quotes are consumed. A raw book snapshot is therefore a structured row rather than a flat tabular observation: for each displayed level it contains a bid price, bid volume, ask price, and ask volume. With twenty displayed levels, one snapshot contains eighty raw book fields before trade-flow and derived features are added. Across time, consecutive snapshots show how queues build, vanish, or move across levels. These changes are the main signal in LOB prediction because they reveal buying and selling pressure before it appears as a mid-price move. Following the multi-level OFI representation of Kolm et al. (2023) , which builds on the order-flow imbalance construction of Cont et al. (2014) , we use OFI as the primary LOB representation. OFI summarizes whether liquidity is added, cancelled, or consumed on the bid and ask sides before the mid-price moves. New bid depth or removed ask depth pushes signed flow positive; removed bid depth or new ask depth pushes it negative. Aggregating these signed changes converts irregular book updates into a regular time-series signal for neural sequence models. Appendix A.1 gives the full LOB notation, Coinbase feature construction, and exact OFI aggregation formula in Eq. ( 10 ). Appendix A.4 reports the train-only heavy-tail diagnostics, including Figures 4 and 5 . The representation-learning question is whether the auxiliary corruption task should match the market residuals seen by OFI windows. Many bins contain small queue adjustments, but active periods can contain abrupt order sweeps, liquidity withdrawals, or bursts of one-sided trading. A pooled Hill/Pareto tail-index estimate on Coinbase OFI magnitudes gives α ^ = 1.62 \hat{\alpha}=1.62 , well below Gaussian light-tail behavior (Appendix A.4 ). A Gaussian denoising task emphasizes a fixed quadratic geometry around the clean input; the non-Gaussian score tasks below instead expose the shared classifier trunk to larger residuals during training. The reverse diffusion chain is never run at inference, so the method is stochastic representation learning rather than a generative market simulator.

sections.heading: 4 Methodology
sections.text: StochLOB is designed to change the training signal while leaving the deployed predictor unchanged. Each minibatch is seen in two views. The clean window x 0 x_{0} is passed through the classifier path and optimized with the ordinary three-class trend loss. A second, stochastically corrupted view x t x_{t} is passed through a score head attached to the same temporal trunk. Only the shared representation is common between these objectives; at test time the noisy view, corruption sampler, score table, and score head are all disabled.

For Coinbase, T = 60 T=60 and F = 31 F=31 : each window covers 10 minutes sampled every 10 seconds. sections.heading: 4.3 Two Market-Shaped Corruptions
sections.text: StochLOB ( Lévy ). The jump variant uses a Brownian background plus a compound-Poisson gamma variance: W t = σ t 2 + ∑ j = 1 N t S j , N t ∼ Poisson ⁡ ( Λ t ) , S j ∼ Gamma ⁡ ( κ , θ ) . W_{t}=\sigma_{t}^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{N_{t}}S_{j},\qquad N_{t}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\Lambda_{t}),\quad S_{j}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\kappa,\theta). (8) This exposes the representation to mostly ordinary perturbations with occasional large shocks, matching the intuition of order sweeps or liquidity withdrawals. StochLOB ( α \alpha -stable). The stable variant uses W t = σ t 2 ​ A , A ∼ 𝒮 α / 2 + , 𝔼 ⁡ [ exp ⁡ ( − s ​ A ) ] = exp ⁡ ( − s α / 2 ) . W_{t}=\sigma_{t}^{2}A,\qquad A\sim\mathcal{S}^{+}_{\alpha/2},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\exp(-sA)]=\exp(-s^{\alpha/2}). (9) This creates polynomial-tail perturbations in the ideal case. The implementation clips A A at a high quantile for numerical stability, giving a truncated-stable corruption law that remains much heavier-tailed than a Gaussian. Appendix A (Data Details, Alpha Selection, and Tail Diagnostics), especially Appendices A.2 and A.3 , explains how α \alpha and α lab \alpha_{\mathrm{lab}} are selected without test leakage.

sections.heading: 4.4 Architecture
sections.text: All proposed variants use the same classifier family: optional BiN normalization, a two-layer bidirectional GRU, one temporal self-attention block with timestep conditioning, attention pooling, and a three-class classifier head. The score head is a training-only branch attached to the shared representation. Figure 2 shows the complete training workflow and the inference path without stochastic corruption. Using a shared architecture isolates the effect of the corruption law: changes in test behavior are attributable to the auxiliary stochastic objective rather than to a larger inference model. Training, inference, and score-table pseudocode are given in Appendix B (GSM Score Table) and Appendix D (Training and Inference Pseudocode). Figure 2 : StochLOB workflow. The classifier pools the unperturbed sequence representation for three trend logits. The training-only score decoder receives the noisy T × F T\times F window, timestep embedding, and per-timestep trunk context, and predicts a T × F T\times F score field. At inference, the corruption sampler and score decoder are disabled.

sections.heading: 5 Datasets
sections.text: We use point-in-time market data from crypto and equity order books. Appendix A gives the exact timestamps, feature construction, normalization, split counts, label calibration, and tail diagnostics. Coinbase crypto. The main benchmark is Coinbase order-book and trade data for BTC, ETH, BNB, XRP, and USDT. The main text focuses on BTC as the deepest symbol; ETH, BNB, XRP, and USDT results are in Appendix E . Feishu A-share universe. Feishu is a broader Chinese A-share transfer setting. Each asset-day combines intraday OFI summaries with daily OHLCV and technical variables. The transfer study evaluates the resulting directional probabilities through a common constrained portfolio rule, described in Appendix F .

sections.heading: 6.1 Experiment Setup
sections.text: All Coinbase experiments use chronological 70/15/15 train, validation, and test splits, so every model is evaluated on later market periods than those used for training. Checkpoints are selected by validation macro-F1 and then frozen for all reported test metrics. The main tables use OFI windows with T = 60 T=60 , F = 31 F=31 , and horizons k ∈ { 10 , 20 , 50 , 100 } k\in\{10,20,50,100\} . Optimizer, corruption, seed-sweep, and Feishu transfer details are given in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 7 Discussion
sections.text: The central message of StochLOB is not that one architecture should dominate every standard benchmark cell. It is that the auxiliary corruption used for representation learning should match the regime in which robustness is needed. Crypto OFI inputs are heavy-tailed, ordinary Gaussian corruption is a limited proxy for market stress, and non-Gaussian score matching gives the shared representation a geometry that is more appropriate for large-residual states. The posterior-precision view of h t h_{t} makes this mechanism explicit: as the residual magnitude changes, the score adapts to the corruption scale that is plausible under the chosen noise law. There are limits. The compound-Poisson law is still isotropic after scaling; real book shocks are signed, level-correlated, and state dependent. The alpha-stable law is clipped for numerical stability, so the implementation is a truncated-stable training distribution rather than a pure infinite-variance process. Feishu also shows that robust probabilities are not automatically portfolio-ready; the alpha-stable model may need threshold or utility-aware calibration before its conservative signal becomes economically useful. Future work should turn this into a sharper coverage criterion. The present corruptions improve radial coverage by making large residual magnitudes plausible during training, but they do not guarantee angular coverage: real book stress is signed, cross-level, and concentrated along a small number of market directions. Appendix G , especially Appendix G.1 , formalizes this with a second-order change-of-measure argument in which robustness transfer depends on both radial tail compatibility and an angular Rényi term that can dominate in high-dimensional LOB windows. This motivates four next steps: estimate state-dependent directional stress spectra and replace scalar h t ​ ( r ) h_{t}(r) with matrix-valued posterior precision; replay signed empirical jumps from real order-book residuals; separate the score loss and temporal readout with multi-seed ablations; and select portfolio thresholds on validation data under transaction costs and risk constraints.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: This work reframes LOB diffusion regularization around the noise geometry observed in market data. StochLOB keeps inference as a deterministic classifier, but trains the shared representation with jump-like or heavy-tailed score-matching corruption. The resulting models remain competitive on standard Coinbase trend prediction, improve several realized stress-window diagnostics, and produce probabilities that can be tested under a constrained Feishu portfolio rule. Appendix G (Posterior-Precision Interpretation of h t h_{t} ) proves that h t h_{t} is a posterior expected corruption precision; Appendices D (Training and Inference Pseudocode) and C (Experimental Setup and Implementation Details) provide the operational details.

sections.text: The Feishu dataset is the larger Chinese A-share protocol used for the portfolio transfer experiment. The feature tensor has 259 coordinates per asset-day. sections.heading: C.1 Shared Architecture
sections.text: Both StochLOB variants use optional BiN normalization, a two-layer bidirectional GRU with 64 hidden units per direction, one DiT-style temporal self-attention block with four heads and adaLN-Zero timestep conditioning, attention pooling for trend classification, and a small convolutional score head. The corruption law and loss differ; the inference path without stochastic corruption is the same. Figure 2 shows the workflow in the main text.

sections.heading: C.2 Optimization
sections.text: Optimization is fixed across the proposed models: AdamW [ Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ] , learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , default moments ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.999) , ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} , weight decay 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , and a per-update schedule with 500 linear warmup steps followed by cosine decay over the planned training steps. We also use gradient clipping at 1.0, label smoothing 0.1, and dropout 0.2. Coinbase runs use batch size 64 and at most 80 epochs with patience 15. Feishu runs use batch size 256 and at most 30 epochs. Checkpoints are selected by validation macro-F1 on unperturbed windows, not by the score loss, because the final deployed model is a classifier. The diffusion auxiliary weight is λ diff = 1.0 \lambda_{\mathrm{diff}}=1.0 . The jump-Poisson setting uses a variance-preserving schedule with T max = 1000 T_{\max}=1000 and gamma jump shape/scale 1. The alpha-stable setting clips the positive stable scale at the 0.999 quantile. All reported Coinbase configuration files set device: "cuda" and use single-GPU workers. The reported training runs and checkpoint artifact repair/validation were carried out on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 worker with 24 GB VRAM. The StochLOB classifier trunk has about 0.53M trainable parameters. Logged per-sample forward costs for the supervised baselines range from effectively zero for linear models to about 0.122 GFLOPs for Axial-LOB; DeepLOB and TLOB are logged at about 0.093 and 0.061 GFLOPs/sample, respectively. The score-table Monte Carlo preprocessing is performed once per corruption law and schedule and is reused by the training runs.

sections.heading: C.3 Crypto Evaluation
sections.text: For each symbol and horizon, all baselines use the same chronological train/validation/test windows, the same feature normalization, and the same train-calibrated label thresholds. Standard held-out metrics are accuracy and macro-F1 on the held-out test interval. The main paper reports BTC; the appendix reports ETH, BNB, XRP, and USDT. Seed-sweep results are reported as mean and sample standard deviation over seeds 13 , 21 , 42 , 84 , 168 13,21,42,84,168 . The realized stress evaluation freezes the trained checkpoint and partitions held-out BTC windows by statistics computed from the observed test inputs. The stress score is the maximum one-step level-averaged feature increment divided by realized volatility; the variance score is the realized variance of those increments; and the jump-residual score is the residual from regressing the largest increment on realized variance in log-log space. This keeps the data split, trained weights, class thresholds, and decision rule fixed while testing the regimes where stochastic score-matching corruption should matter.

sections.heading: C.4 Feishu Evaluation
sections.text: Feishu uses a two-year in-sample period and one-year out-of-sample release period. The in-sample period is split chronologically per asset into train/validation windows. The out-of-sample period is never used for label thresholds, normalization decisions, checkpoint selection, or trading threshold selection. Model probabilities are exported day by day and consumed by the common portfolio engine described in Appendix F .

sections.heading: F.1 Models and Prediction Targets
sections.text: Every Feishu model is trained to predict the same three-class next-period mid-price trend target: y ∈ { down , flat , up } . y\in\{\mathrm{down},\mathrm{flat},\mathrm{up}\}. The portfolio experiment does not introduce a separate trading model. It uses the classifier probabilities ( P ⁡ ( down ) , P ⁡ ( flat ) , P ⁡ ( up ) ) (P(\mathrm{down}),P(\mathrm{flat}),P(\mathrm{up})) as alpha signals. This makes the downstream transfer test direct: if the learned probabilities contain useful directional information, a constrained portfolio rule should be able to convert them into positive out-of-sample performance. The experiment is therefore a check of probability usability, not a claim that the paper designs a deployable trading system.

sections.heading: F.2 Portfolio Construction
sections.text: The Feishu portfolio experiment uses the out-of-sample release period only for the exploratory portfolio evaluation. In-sample data are used as causal warmup history for rolling features such as returns, volatility, RSI, and the 5-day OFI normalizer. For each model and each trading day t t , the signal is computed from the historical window ending at t − 1 t-1 . The portfolio rule receives ( P ⁡ ( down ) , P ⁡ ( flat ) , P ⁡ ( up ) ) (P(\mathrm{down}),P(\mathrm{flat}),P(\mathrm{up})) and converts the probabilities into positions. Assets with sufficiently high up probability are eligible for buying, while assets with sufficiently high down probability are eligible for partial selling. The backtest uses an initial capital of RMB 50 million. The same constraints are applied to every model: 100-share lot size, commission rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , stamp-duty rate 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} on sells, RMB 5 minimum commission, T+1 sell lock, a 5% cash buffer, and a minimum-holdings target of 10 names. These rules matter for Chinese A-share data. A signal that is statistically useful but unstable can create high turnover and cost drag; a signal that is too conservative can fail to trade. The portfolio experiment therefore measures whether the model output remains usable after realistic market constraints. The daily rule has three steps. First, held assets are examined for exit. A held asset is fully sold when P ⁡ ( down ) > 0.85 P(\mathrm{down})>0.85 and the predicted class is down, subject to the T+1 sell lock and the minimum-holdings constraint. If a held asset is predicted flat and was not already fully sold, the strategy sells 50% of the sellable shares. Second, new buys are selected from assets with P ⁡ ( up ) > 0.75 P(\mathrm{up})>0.75 and predicted class up. Third, available capital after the 5% cash buffer is allocated equally across the selected buy candidates. Orders are rounded to 100-share lots, buy executions use the morning VWAP entry price, and sell executions use the configured close-price sell mode. The model therefore controls which assets are traded, while the portfolio engine keeps sizing and market rules common across all methods. We also include a passive equal-weight index. On each out-of-sample day it holds all valid assets equally and applies the same one-day VWAP-entry-to-close return convention. It is not an active trading strategy and it does not pay transaction costs in this implementation. Its purpose is to show whether a learned signal adds value relative to broad market exposure.

sections.heading: F.3 Out-of-Sample Portfolio Metrics
sections.text: The main out-of-sample portfolio metrics are reported in Table 3 , and the cumulative-return comparison is shown in Figure 3 . We keep the numeric table in the main text because it is the economic summary most directly connected to the experimental story. This appendix gives the construction details needed to interpret those numbers. The most important implementation point is that the portfolio engine is shared across models. A model can improve the backtest only by changing the probability triplet used for buy, hold, and sell decisions; it cannot change position sizing, execution prices, transaction-cost assumptions, or market constraints. In the reported run, several evaluated architectures produced mostly flat predictions during the out-of-sample window and therefore did not produce meaningful active portfolios under the common thresholds. These inactive runs are omitted from Table 3 so that the main comparison focuses on strategies that actually trade.

They do not imply that every non-Gaussian corruption must improve macro-F1. Instead, they show that the proposed non-Gaussian objectives possess a family-level residual-adaptation mechanism that the Gaussian baseline cannot possess. This interpretation is complementary to recent work that replaces Gaussian perturbations by heavy-tailed or Lévy alternatives in denoising score matching and diffusion models [ Deasy et al., 2021 , Yoon et al., 2023 , Pandey et al., 2025 , Shariatian et al., 2025 ] : rather than proposing a new generative reverse process, the analysis here isolates the posterior-precision mechanism induced by the latent scale in the supervised StochLOB objective. The stress experiments determine whether these structural properties are useful for the observed LOB prediction problem.

Abstract Score-based diffusion methods usually perturb data with Brownian Gaussian noise, corresponding to a light-tailed forward stochastic differential equation (SDE). For market time series this SDE can be a poor abstraction: limit order book (LOB) order flow is heavy-tailed, bursty, and occasionally jump-like. We study StochLOB , a training-only score-matching framework that changes the forward diffusion corruption law while leaving the deployed predictor deterministic. Instead of Brownian-only Gaussian corruption, the noising process uses two non-Gaussian SDE-inspired alternatives: jump- Lévy noise through a compound-Poisson variance mixture, and clipped α \alpha -stable noise through a positive-stable Gaussian scale mixture. These corruptions inject finite jumps and heavy-tailed residuals into training without requiring reverse-time diffusion sampling at inference. The resulting score target has a useful interpretation: its radial factor h t ​ ( r ) h_{t}(r) is the posterior expected corruption precision, so large residuals are weighted according to the latent corruption scale that most plausibly generated them. On chronologically held-out Coinbase LOB data, the proposed variants remain competitive on uncorrupted BTC and altcoin test horizons and improve several realized tail-window stress diagnostics. An exploratory Feishu A-share transfer study further tests whether the probability outputs remain usable under transaction costs and trading-rule constraints. Code and configuration files are available at https://github.com/ArshiAbolghasemi/Penny . 1 Introduction Score-based diffusion methods are commonly built around a Brownian forward stochastic differential equation (SDE), whose finite-time corruption is Gaussian and light-tailed. This modeling choice is convenient, but it also defines the residual geometry seen by a denoising score objective: large coordinate movements become exponentially unlikely, and the learned restoring force is tied to a Brownian quadratic penalty. For data generated by stochastic systems with bursts, jumps, or persistent heavy tails, the Brownian-only SDE can therefore be a poor training corruption law. Limit order book (LOB) prediction makes this mismatch concrete. Order-flow imbalance (OFI), depth changes, and short-horizon returns can remain quiet for many bins and then move abruptly after an order sweep, a liquidity withdrawal, or a short burst of directional trading. These large residuals are not rare under the market process, but they are rare under Gaussian diffusion corruption. This is difficult to reconcile with the heavy tails and jump-like behavior observed in financial time series and LOB order flow ( Mandelbrot, 1963 ; Cont, 2001 ; Cont et al., 2014 ) . The question we study is whether the forward diffusion SDE used for score-based regularization should be modified so its noise law better matches the stochastic input process. We introduce StochLOB , a training-only framework for robust mid-price trend prediction. The deployed model remains a standard classifier: the corruption sampler and score head are used only while learning the shared representation, and test-time inference is a single deterministic forward pass. This isolates the effect of changing the stochastic diffusion corruption from the cost of reverse-time diffusion sampling at deployment. We consider two non-Gaussian SDE-inspired corruption families. The jump- Lévy variant adds a compound-Poisson jump component to a Brownian background, implemented as a Gaussian scale mixture that exposes the representation to mostly ordinary perturbations with occasional finite jumps. The α \alpha -stable variant replaces the fixed Brownian variance with a clipped positive-stable scale mixture, producing broad heavy-tailed perturbations while retaining numerical stability. Both variants use the same classifier architecture and differ only in the stochastic training law and auxiliary loss. The score target is also interpretable: the radial score factor h t ​ ( r ) h_{t}(r) is a posterior precision under the latent corruption scale. Thus the denoising objective does not apply the same restoring force to every residual. Ordinary residuals receive high posterior precision, while extreme residuals can be explained by larger latent corruption scales. Our empirical analysis follows the same logic. First, distribution-fit and tail diagnostics on Coinbase OFI show that the Gaussian assumption is a poor description of the observed inputs. Second, on Coinbase BTC and four additional crypto symbols, the proposed variants remain competitive on standard held-out mid-price trend prediction and win selected horizons, showing that the stochastic auxiliary objective does not require a large standard-test accuracy tradeoff. Third, realized stress-window diagnostics evaluate the regimes that motivate the method: high-stress, high-variance, and jump-residual windows in which Gaussian corruption is least plausible. Figure 1 gives the headline stress diagnostic at k = 100 k=100 . We also include an exploratory Feishu A-share transfer study in which model probabilities are converted into constrained portfolio signals, checking whether the forecasts remain useful after transaction costs, lot-size rules, and T+1 selling constraints. This transfer check is not meant to define a complete trading system; it tests whether the learned probabilities survive a realistic downstream decision rule. Contributions. We make three contributions. First, we formulate robust supervised representation learning as a mismatch between Brownian diffusion-SDE corruption and heavy-tailed, jump-like stochastic inputs, using LOB trend prediction as the concrete test bed. Second, we modify the training-time diffusion corruption with jump- Lévy and clipped α \alpha -stable noise while keeping the LOB predictor deterministic and free of inference-time sampling. Third, we provide a posterior-precision interpretation of the resulting score function h t h_{t} , with proofs and future-work mathematics in Appendix G . Appendices A – F provide the data details, score-table construction, implementation and training algorithms, additional crypto results, and the Feishu portfolio analysis. Figure 1 : Main stress result on chronologically held-out Coinbase BTC windows at horizon k = 100 k=100 ( 31,842 31{,}842 test windows). Columns sort windows by realized stress, realized variance, and variance-controlled jump residual, all computed from one-step increments of the level-averaged feature stream. Decile 10 is the most turbulent. The top row reports macro-F1 by decile; the bottom row reports paired differences against the same StochLOB trunk trained with cross-entropy only. Shaded bands are 95 % 95\% circular block-bootstrap confidence intervals. 2 Related Work LOB trend prediction. LOB forecasting has moved from linear models toward architectures that exploit both level structure and temporal order. DeepLOB combines convolutional, Inception, and recurrent blocks for mid-price movement prediction ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) . TABL and BiN-TABL add bilinear mappings, temporal attention, and input normalization for financial time series ( Tran et al., 2019 ; Tran et al., 2021 ) . Later work studies stronger attention and benchmarking designs, including TLOB, LiT, LOBench, Axial-LOB, and order-flow attention networks ( Berti and Kasneci, 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2025 ; Kisiel and Gorse, 2022 ; Bandealinaeini et al., 2025 ) . Our experiments keep the standard three-class mid-price trend protocol and compare against linear, recurrent, convolutional-attention, transformer, and single-asset order-flow attention baselines trained on the same chronological windows. Heavy tails and jumps. Heavy tails are a classical stylized fact of financial returns ( Mandelbrot, 1963 ; Cont, 2001 ) ; LOB-specific studies show non-Gaussian behavior in liquidity, impact, and order flow ( Bouchaud et al., 2002 ; Mike and Farmer, 2008 ; Gould et al., 2013 ; Cont et al., 2014 ) . Jump-diffusion models provide a finite-activity language for abrupt price moves ( Merton, 1976 ) , while stable processes model persistent heavy-tailed fluctuations ( Samorodnitsky and Taqqu, 1994 ) . We use these objects as training-time corruption laws, not as complete market simulators. Diffusion as representation learning. Score-based and denoising diffusion models are typically introduced as generative models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) , but the denoising task can also shape supervised representations. Joint diffusion training uses shared networks for denoising and prediction ( Deja et al., 2023 ) , and related work studies diffusion features as representation learners ( Yang and Wang, 2023 ) . Non-Gaussian diffusion replaces Brownian noise with jump or heavy-tailed processes ( Yoon et al., 2023 ; Shariatian et al., 2025 ; Pandey et al., 2025 ) . LOB diffusion work models event streams, counterfactual books, or volume snapshots ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Wang and Ventre, 2026 ; Wang and Ventre, 2025 ) ; StochLOB instead uses non-Gaussian corruption as a training-time auxiliary regularizer for deterministic LOB classification. 3 Background Limit order book (LOB) data record the outstanding limit orders waiting at an exchange. At any time, the book has a bid side, where traders are willing to buy, and an ask side, where traders are willing to sell. Each side is ordered by price into levels: the first bid and ask levels are the immediately executable quotes, while deeper levels describe nearby liquidity that would be reached after the top quotes are consumed. A raw book snapshot is therefore a structured row rather than a flat tabular observation: for each displayed level it contains a bid price, bid volume, ask price, and ask volume. With twenty displayed levels, one snapshot contains eighty raw book fields before trade-flow and derived features are added. Across time, consecutive snapshots show how queues build, vanish, or move across levels. These changes are the main signal in LOB prediction because they reveal buying and selling pressure before it appears as a mid-price move. Following the multi-level OFI representation of Kolm et al. (2023) , which builds on the order-flow imbalance construction of Cont et al. (2014) , we use OFI as the primary LOB representation. OFI summarizes whether liquidity is added, cancelled, or consumed on the bid and ask sides before the mid-price moves. New bid depth or removed ask depth pushes signed flow positive; removed bid depth or new ask depth pushes it negative. Aggregating these signed changes converts irregular book updates into a regular time-series signal for neural sequence models. Appendix A.1 gives the full LOB notation, Coinbase feature construction, and exact OFI aggregation formula in Eq. ( 10 ). Appendix A.4 reports the train-only heavy-tail diagnostics, including Figures 4 and 5 . The representation-learning question is whether the auxiliary corruption task should match the market residuals seen by OFI windows. Many bins contain small queue adjustments, but active periods can contain abrupt order sweeps, liquidity withdrawals, or bursts of one-sided trading. A pooled Hill/Pareto tail-index estimate on Coinbase OFI magnitudes gives α ^ = 1.62 \hat{\alpha}=1.62 , well below Gaussian light-tail behavior (Appendix A.4 ). A Gaussian denoising task emphasizes a fixed quadratic geometry around the clean input; the non-Gaussian score tasks below instead expose the shared classifier trunk to larger residuals during training. The reverse diffusion chain is never run at inference, so the method is stochastic representation learning rather than a generative market simulator. 4 Methodology StochLOB is designed to change the training signal while leaving the deployed predictor unchanged. Each minibatch is seen in two views. The clean window x 0 x_{0} is passed through the classifier path and optimized with the ordinary three-class trend loss. A second, stochastically corrupted view x t x_{t} is passed through a score head attached to the same temporal trunk. Only the shared representation is common between these objectives; at test time the noisy view, corruption sampler, score table, and score head are all disabled. 4.1 Problem and Labels Given a normalized LOB feature window x 0 ∈ ℝ T × F x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times F} , the classifier returns probabilities over { down , stationary , up } \{\mathrm{down},\mathrm{stationary},\mathrm{up}\} . For Coinbase, T = 60 T=60 and F = 31 F=31 : each window covers 10 minutes sampled every 10 seconds. Windows are therefore assigned to train, validation, or test only when the full look-back context and the full future label horizon remain inside the same split. We choose Gaussian scale mixtures because they keep the score target tractable while allowing non-Gaussian residuals. Conditional on W t = w W_{t}=w , the corruption is Gaussian and isotropic. Marginally, however, the variance is random, so the residual distribution can place much more probability on large moves. This gives a controlled way to expose the classifier representation to market-shaped perturbations without changing the input schema or the inference-time architecture. The jump variant uses a Brownian background plus a compound-Poisson gamma variance: W t = σ t 2 + ∑ j = 1 N t S j , N t ∼ Poisson ⁡ ( Λ t ) , S j ∼ Gamma ⁡ ( κ , θ ) . W_{t}=\sigma_{t}^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{N_{t}}S_{j},\qquad N_{t}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\Lambda_{t}),\quad S_{j}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\kappa,\theta). (8) This exposes the representation to mostly ordinary perturbations with occasional large shocks, matching the intuition of order sweeps or liquidity withdrawals. StochLOB ( α \alpha -stable). The implementation clips A A at a high quantile for numerical stability, giving a truncated-stable corruption law that remains much heavier-tailed than a Gaussian. Appendix A (Data Details, Alpha Selection, and Tail Diagnostics), especially Appendices A.2 and A.3 , explains how α \alpha and α lab \alpha_{\mathrm{lab}} are selected without test leakage. 4.4 Architecture All proposed variants use the same classifier family: optional BiN normalization, a two-layer bidirectional GRU, one temporal self-attention block with timestep conditioning, attention pooling, and a three-class classifier head. The score head is a training-only branch attached to the shared representation. Figure 2 shows the complete training workflow and the inference path without stochastic corruption. Using a shared architecture isolates the effect of the corruption law: changes in test behavior are attributable to the auxiliary stochastic objective rather than to a larger inference model. Training, inference, and score-table pseudocode are given in Appendix B (GSM Score Table) and Appendix D (Training and Inference Pseudocode). Figure 2 : StochLOB workflow. The training-only score decoder receives the noisy T × F T\times F window, timestep embedding, and per-timestep trunk context, and predicts a T × F T\times F score field. It is that the auxiliary corruption used for representation learning should match the regime in which robustness is needed. Crypto OFI inputs are heavy-tailed, ordinary Gaussian corruption is a limited proxy for market stress, and non-Gaussian score matching gives the shared representation a geometry that is more appropriate for large-residual states. The posterior-precision view of h t h_{t} makes this mechanism explicit: as the residual magnitude changes, the score adapts to the corruption scale that is plausible under the chosen noise law. There are limits. The compound-Poisson law is still isotropic after scaling; real book shocks are signed, level-correlated, and state dependent. The alpha-stable law is clipped for numerical stability, so the implementation is a truncated-stable training distribution rather than a pure infinite-variance process. Feishu also shows that robust probabilities are not automatically portfolio-ready; the alpha-stable model may need threshold or utility-aware calibration before its conservative signal becomes economically useful. Future work should turn this into a sharper coverage criterion. The present corruptions improve radial coverage by making large residual magnitudes plausible during training, but they do not guarantee angular coverage: real book stress is signed, cross-level, and concentrated along a small number of market directions. Appendix G , especially Appendix G.1 , formalizes this with a second-order change-of-measure argument in which robustness transfer depends on both radial tail compatibility and an angular Rényi term that can dominate in high-dimensional LOB windows. This motivates four next steps: estimate state-dependent directional stress spectra and replace scalar h t ​ ( r ) h_{t}(r) with matrix-valued posterior precision; replay signed empirical jumps from real order-book residuals; separate the score loss and temporal readout with multi-seed ablations; and select portfolio thresholds on validation data under transaction costs and risk constraints. 8 Conclusion This work reframes LOB diffusion regularization around the noise geometry observed in market data. StochLOB keeps inference as a deterministic classifier, but trains the shared representation with jump-like or heavy-tailed score-matching corruption. The resulting models remain competitive on standard Coinbase trend prediction, improve several realized stress-window diagnostics, and produce probabilities that can be tested under a constrained Feishu portfolio rule.
